newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - January 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - January 30.

text.p: Following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Thursday.
- The British government seems set to opt for a phased implementation of the recommendations of the Northern Ireland report on parades and marches, to be published in Belfast on Thursday morning.
- The decision to allow the Orange march at Drumcree "damaged the RUC's reputation as an impartial police force", according to a U.S. government report on human rights to be published on Thursday.
- Irish mortgadge lenders are overcharging their customers by 60 to 80 million Irish pounds per annum, according to a study carried out by REA Mortgage Services.
- The Japanese car group Toyota has warned that future levels of investment in Britain could be affected if the UK stayed outside Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
- Enterprise Minister Richard Bruton on Wednesday night ordered a wide-ranging investigation of drink prices including possible cartel-style price fixing by some publicans.

- The three-year Partnership 2000 pay pact will on Thursday be ratified by a special Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) conference following a stronger than expected majority in favour from the largest union SIPTU.
- Unemployed people are to be asked to fill short-term jobs in the public service under a radical new work-sharing plan.
- Total repeal of the draconian Official Secrets Act is recommended by a powerful Irish parliamentary committee in a report yet to be published.
- Bank of Ireland has appointed a senior executive to oversee its planning for EMU, moving into line with its main competetors, Ulster Bank and AIB.
- A breakthrough in the long-running row between two police representative bodies is likely following conciliatory moves, including the defferal of a High Court action.
- Four hundred workers at Irish Life are to be suspended without pay from next Monday following a four to one vote by the union on Wednesday night rejecting Labour Court recommendations.

- Tough talking is expected when a high level negotiating team from the Irish League of Credit Unions sits down with senior Department of Enterprise and Employment officials next week in a determined bid to get key parts of the controversial Credit Union Bill changed.
